module_title: Advanced Analysis - Continental Drift and Ocean Floor Relief
introduction: This advanced level explores one of the greatest theories in geology: Continental Drift. We will also look beneath the surface of the oceans to understand 'Oceanic Relief', proving that the ocean floor is not a flat bathtub but a complex landscape of submerged mountains and deep valleys.

core_concepts.title: Continental Drift Theory
core_concepts.description: Proposed by meteorologist 'Alfred Wegener' in 1912. Wegener theorized that millions of years ago, all current continents were joined together in a single, massive super-continent called 'Pangaea'. This landmass was surrounded by a single global super-ocean called 'Panthalassa'.

core_concepts.title: Laurasia and Gondwanaland
core_concepts.description: Around 200 million years ago, Pangaea broke into two massive landmasses. The northern block was called 'Laurasia' (comprising North America, Europe, and Asia). The southern block was called 'Gondwanaland' (comprising South America, Africa, India, Australia, and Antarctica). The shallow sea that formed between them was the 'Tethys Sea'.

core_concepts.title: Ocean Floor Relief
core_concepts.description: Moving from the coast into the deep ocean, the floor is divided into 4 main relief features: 1. Continental Shelf - The shallow submerged edge of a continent (rich in fish and petroleum). 2. Continental Slope - The steep drop-off. 3. Abyssal Plains - The vast, deep, flat ocean floor. 4. Oceanic Trenches - The deep, narrow, tectonic canyons.

core_concepts.title: Mid-Oceanic Ridges
core_concepts.description: These are massive, continuous underwater mountain ranges formed by volcanic activity where tectonic plates are pulling apart (divergent boundaries). The 'Mid-Atlantic Ridge' is the longest mountain range in the world, completely submerged underwater.

important_entities.name: The 'S' Shape of the Atlantic
important_entities.significance: The Atlantic Ocean has a distinct 'S' shape. It is flanked by North and South America on the west, and Europe and Africa on the east. Due to the highly indented coastline which provides excellent natural harbors, it is the 'busiest' ocean in the world for trade and commerce.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: The Origin of the Indian Peninsula
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A critical UPSC/PCS trap: Because India is currently in Asia, students assume it was part of the northern super-continent 'Laurasia'. This is completely false. The Indian Peninsula was originally a part of the southern 'Gondwanaland'. It broke off, drifted northwards for millions of years, and violently crashed into the Eurasian plate, which gave birth to the Himalayas.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: The southern block broke into: South America, Africa, India, Australia, and Antarctica. (North America and Eurasia belonged to Laurasia).

exam_strategy_tips: Link the theory to the scientist: Continental Drift = Alfred Wegener. This is a direct, highly-tested fact.
Always remember that the mighty Himalayas stand today exactly where the ancient 'Tethys Sea' used to exist.
